Honestly, no — I don't think that framing is more accurate. "Both have merits, depends on the individual" is the kind of thing that sounds fair but actually dodges the question. Sometimes one position is just better supported than the other, and flattening that into false balance isn't honesty, it's avoidance.

That said, I can acknowledge genuine nuance: some roles do benefit from in-person work (lab work, hands-on onboarding, certain creative collisions), and some people genuinely prefer offices. But the overall direction of the evidence still favors remote-first for most knowledge work. I'm not going to pretend I don't have a view just because a softer one would be more palatable.
